units.translation: 2. αὐτός is, but only in oblique cases, and not at the beginning of a sentence, but after one or more words, and mostly in dialogue, more rarely in lyric passages, just as among the Latins also eius, ei, eum were considered alien to more elevated poetry, about which Bentley spoke on Horace's Odes 3, 11, 18 quamvis furiale centum muniant angues caput eius.

3. αὐτός joined with the article, ὁ αὐτός, ἡ αὐτή, τὸ αὐτό means the same, which are not rarely contracted by crasis into αὑτός, αυτή, ταυτό or ταυτόν. Of these the first two are very often written in the manuscripts of the scenic poets with smooth breathing, αὐτός and αὐτή, about which we give a general warning here. In Aeschylus
